meta.title: Who really said "Let Us Make a Special Effort to Stop Communicating with Each Other, So We Can Have Some Conversation"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Mark Twain, who died in 1910. Judith Martin wrote it as Miss Manners in 1979 — and a 1999 insult anthology is where the credit slipped.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Let Us Make a Special Effort to Stop Communicating with Each Other, So We Can Have Some Conversation'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator traces it to Judith Martin’s 1979 Miss Manners column. The Twain credit came from a quote printed next to it in a 1999 book.

answer.label: Not Mark Twain — Judith Martin, writing as Miss Manners
answer.sourceLine: Mark Twain died in 1910 and there is no evidence he wrote this. Quote Investigator ↗ traces it to Judith Martin, whose syndicated “Miss Manners” column of September 1979 opened: “The new social season being now upon us, let us make a special effort to learn to stop communicating with one another, so that we can have some conversation.” The version in circulation drops “to learn” and swaps “one another” for “each other”.

source.excerpt: The new social season being now upon us, let us make a special effort to learn to stop communicating with one another, so that we can have some conversation.
trail: We read Quote Investigator’s article ↗ in full. It finds no substantive evidence for Twain and notes the line is absent from Barbara Schmidt’s TwainQuotes.com, the standard checking tool for Twain ascriptions.

QI’s earliest citation is the 1979 Miss Manners column, printed in The Bulletin of Bend, Oregon on 1 September 1979 at page 19 and in the State Times Advocate of Baton Rouge on 3 September 1979 at page 3B.

The same sentence, in the longer form, reappears in Miss Manners’ Guide to Excruciatingly Correct Behavior — QI cites page 165 of the 1983 Warner Books reprint of the 1982 Atheneum edition, verified with scans.

We checked Wikiquote directly in both directions: the Mark Twain page ↗ has no entry for this line in any section, and the Judith Martin page ↗ does not carry it either — so the only documentary trail runs through QI’s newspaper citations.
source.excerptNote: That is Martin’s opening sentence as Quote Investigator reproduces it from the 1979 column. The familiar version is shorter by two words and swaps one pronoun — the sort of smoothing that makes a line easier to repeat and easier to lose track of.

source.rightsNote: First published in a syndicated newspaper column in 1979 and reprinted in a 1982 book, both far later than the 1931 boundary for U.S. public domain. The text belongs to Judith Martin and her syndicate and publishers. The misattribution to Mark Twain, whose own work is largely public domain, is probably part of why people assume this line is free to use.

author.heading: About Judith Martin
author.metaLine: born 13 September 1938 · American columnist and etiquette authority
author.bio: Judith Martin (born 1938) is an American journalist who has written the syndicated etiquette column Miss Manners since 1978, after years as a reporter and critic at the Washington Post. Writing in a mock-formal third person, she treats manners as a serious subject and modern candour as a menace, and has turned the column into a long shelf of books.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook case of a misattribution with a traceable mechanism — not a vague drift, but a specific page in a specific book where the wrong name was sitting one line away.

items.why: Twain died in 1910, sixty-nine years before the earliest instance Quote Investigator ↗ could find. QI also reports the line is absent from TwainQuotes.com, the reference database it treats as the checkpoint for Twain ascriptions.

On page 130 of Tom Steele’s anthology the simplified sentence appears credited to Miss Manners, directly beneath a Twain quotation about good breeding. QI’s reading ↗ is that a reader looking up for the attribution instead of down carried Twain’s name onto Martin’s line.

items.who: “…stop communicating with each other, so we can have some conversation”
items.why: That 1999 anthology is also where the words “to learn” were dropped. Martin wrote “learn to stop communicating with one another, so that we can have some conversation”.
QI records the Twain-credited version circulating on the Quoteland forum by 2003, unvetted by the site’s administrators — an ordinary step in how an anthology slip becomes an internet fact.

misattribution.truthLine: Judith Martin wrote it as Miss Manners in September 1979, and Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the Twain credit was manufactured by a 1999 anthology’s page layout.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Martin’s column was needling a very 1970s habit: the therapeutic imperative to communicate, meaning to disclose everything about yourself to anyone standing nearby. Her joke was that this had replaced conversation rather than improved it.
The rest of the column makes the target obvious. People in communication mode, she wrote, “tell everything about themselves with complete honesty, holding back nothing except their last names”.
detailsBody: Judith Martin began the Miss Manners column in 1978 at the Washington Post, where she had been a reporter and critic. It has run in syndication ever since, and the deadpan third-person voice is the joke as much as the advice is.

The line is now quoted constantly about social media — which it predates by roughly three decades. Its survival is a fair test of Martin’s point, since it mostly travels stripped of its author and half its wording.
context.pull: “Holding back nothing except their last names.”

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator finds no substantive evidence Mark Twain said or wrote this, notes it is absent from TwainQuotes.com, and concludes it originated with Judith Martin as Miss Manners.
QI’s earliest citation is the 1 September 1979 Bulletin (Bend, Oregon) printing of the Miss Manners column at page 19, column 1, and the sentence reads “learn to stop communicating with one another”.
Wikiquote’s Mark Twain page carries no entry for this quotation in any section.
Judith Martin was born on 13 September 1938 and writes as Miss Manners.
